title: Make Time: How to Focus on What Matters Every Day
author: Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky
target_audience: Busy professionals seeking practical time management tactics
Individuals overwhelmed by distractions and digital devices
Anyone aiming to improve focus and prioritize personal goals
Readers interested in work-life balance and intentional living
core_themes: Intentional focus in a world of constant distraction
Practical strategies for reducing digital and environmental interruptions
Experimenting with daily habits to discover what works personally
Prioritizing meaningful work over urgent but less important tasks
Small, repeatable changes leading to sustainable results
primary_purpose: To provide readers with actionable strategies and simple tactics to help reclaim their attention, prioritize what truly matters each day, and break free from the cycle of busyness and distraction.

structure_format.organization: Four-part framework — Highlight, Laser, Energize, Reflect — with over 80 short, standalone tactics readers can mix and match
features: Personal stories and experiments from the authors

key_concepts_lessons: Choose a single daily priority (the 'Highlight') to focus on meaningful progress.
Manage attention through focused, intentional work instead of relying solely on traditional time management tactics.
Reduce distractions by redesigning phone, email, and social media use.
Boost personal energy by adjusting routines around sleep, diet, movement, and mentality.
Iterate and refine your approach through regular self-reflection.
Small, consistent experiments with new habits can lead to significant, lasting change.
notable_features: Uses real-world experiments and stories, not just theory
Suitable for adaptation to each reader’s personal context
Diverse tactics for focus, energy, and reflection
cultural_historical_context: Released during a period of heightened awareness around digital distraction, social media overuse, and burnout in the workplace. Stands out from traditional productivity books by focusing on making time for what’s important instead of just optimizing schedules.
reception_impact: Positive reviews for practical, flexible advice and engaging style
Popular among readers tired of complex productivity systems
Praised for focus on personal experimentation and sustainable changes
Recommended by leaders and tech workers for its actionable tactics
comparable_titles: The One Thing by Gary Keller and Jay Papasan
